Continual pretraining asks a model to absorb a new corpus — clinical notes, legal filings, code, etc. — without destroying the grammatical, factual, and reasoning scaffolding built during general pretraining. The central question here is precise: does the shape of the learning rate warmup (linear ramp vs. cosine vs. constant-then-decay, and over how many steps) change the degree to which domain gradients overwrite general-language weights, and if so, through what mechanism? The key concepts are gradient interference (domain and general gradients pointing in conflicting directions in weight space), catastrophic forgetting (the well-known failure mode), and the less-discussed interference asymmetry — domain-specific layers (late MLP blocks, embedding rows for rare tokens) are hit harder than syntactic layers, so aggregate perplexity on general text can look fine while structured reasoning silently degrades. What a beginner misses is that warmup geometry isn't just an optimization stability trick; it acts as an implicit regularizer on which parameter subspaces get updated first and most aggressively, meaning a steep early ramp can commit the model to a narrow domain manifold before the optimizer has seen enough gradient diversity to negotiate a compromise. The expert worry is that standard eval benchmarks (perplexity on held-out domain text, MMLU accuracy) are too coarse to detect this — the damage shows up in cross-domain transfer, multi-step reasoning under distribution shift, and instruction-following that relies on priors laid down in general pretraining.

The core implication is that early gradient steps under a steep warmup act like a fast Fourier transform biased toward high-frequency, domain-specific signal — they update attention QK projections and late MLP weights first and hardest, precisely the subspaces that encode factual associations and token co-occurrence statistics from general pretraining. Layer-wise adaptive rate scaling (LARS/LAMB) and its descendants address part of this, but they were designed for batch-size scaling, not domain shift, so they don't selectively protect the early transformer blocks where positional and syntactic priors live. The naive "same LR everywhere" approach is dangerous in the first few hundred steps because the domain corpus gradient variance is highest then — the optimizer hasn't yet averaged over enough domain examples to produce stable gradient directions, so large uniform steps during warmup produce outsized, noisy updates that land far from the general-pretraining optimum in exactly the layers hardest to recover. The practical analog in large-scale continual pretraining is layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD), where earlier layers get rates 10–30× smaller than later layers; values like a decay factor of 0.85–0.9 per layer are common in BERT-era work, but the interaction with warmup length is underexplored — a short warmup with LLRD may be strictly worse than a long warmup without it if the late layers saturate before the early layers have seen meaningful gradient signal. What the expert fears concretely is a regime where the loss curve looks healthy — smooth descent, no spikes — while the model is quietly collapsing onto a domain-specific attractor in weight space from which general-task recovery requires retraining from scratch.

Fisher Information geometry tells us that the weights most at risk are those with high diagonal Fisher entries on general-pretraining data — these are the weights the model relied on most confidently for its general predictions, meaning a domain gradient that moves them even modestly produces large KL divergence from the general-pretrained distribution. This is the foundation of Elastic Weight Consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), which penalizes movement in high-Fisher weights quadratically; the key empirical finding was that in neural networks the Fisher is highly sparse and skewed — a small fraction of weights carry the bulk of the information, and those tend to cluster in attention output projections and the first MLP layer, not uniformly across depth. The empirical Fisher (using sampled gradients from a finite general-pretraining batch rather than the true Fisher) is tractable as a diagonal approximation at BERT/GPT-2 scale, but at LLM scale — 7B+ parameters — storing even the diagonal requires tens of gigabytes, and more critically the diagonal approximation becomes increasingly misleading because off-diagonal correlations (captured by the Kronecker-factored approximation, K-FAC) account for a growing share of the geometry. FISH Mask (Sung et al., 2021) showed a practical middle path: compute a sparse binary mask of the top-0.5% highest-Fisher weights and freeze only those during fine-tuning, achieving near-full EWC protection at a fraction of the memory cost, but this was validated at 100M–1B parameter scale and the mask's stability under distribution shift at 70B scale is an open question. The deeper breakdown at LLM scale is that the empirical Fisher estimated on general-pretraining data is computed at a different point in loss landscape than where continual pretraining begins — if the domain corpus shifts the model even slightly before you compute your protection signal, you're regularizing around the wrong optimum, and with a steep warmup that shift happens in the first dozen steps before any protection is active.

The most concrete data-side intervention is replay mixing — maintaining a fixed proportion of general-pretraining data in every training batch throughout domain adaptation — and the ratio matters enormously: Scialom et al. (2022) on continual learning for NLP found that even 5% replay was disproportionately protective relative to its compute cost, while dropping below 1% produced catastrophic forgetting at rates indistinguishable from no replay at all. The sequencing variant — curriculum ordering rather than random mixing — offers an additional lever: starting the warmup window with batches that are maximally similar to general pretraining (e.g., high-overlap perplexity under the base model) and gradually shifting toward pure domain text forces the optimizer to traverse a smoother path through weight space, effectively substituting data geometry for weight-space regularization. Google's PaLM 2 technical report (Anil et al., 2023) is instructive here: their mixture weights across data sources were tuned as a primary hyperparameter and held roughly constant throughout training rather than staged, which implicitly acts as continuous replay, and they reported that deviating from carefully tuned static mixture ratios degraded both domain performance and general benchmarks — suggesting the stability of the mixture signal matters as much as its composition. The mechanism by which data mixing substitutes for Fisher regularization is gradient direction averaging: if each batch contains both domain and general examples, the net gradient is a convex combination of the two gradient fields, which geometrically prevents the optimizer from fully committing to domain-only directions during the vulnerable early steps when gradient variance is highest. The critical failure mode that experts worry about is frequency mismatch — domain corpora are often orders of magnitude smaller than general pretraining data, so naive mixing at 50/50 means the model sees domain examples tens of times per epoch while general examples are seen once, and the resulting repetition-driven overfitting to domain surface statistics can be worse than pure domain training because it combines memorization pressure with destabilized general gradients.

Within a gradient accumulation window, order absolutely matters in ways that mixing ratio cannot fix: if you accumulate N domain micro-batches before a single general micro-batch and then apply one optimizer step, the effective gradient is dominated by the last few micro-batches due to the non-commutativity of sequential gradient updates when using adaptive optimizers like Adam — the second-moment estimate (v_t) is updated incrementally, so late micro-batches in the accumulation window have disproportionate influence on the adaptive scaling of each parameter. This is not a theoretical nicety; Defazio et al. and subsequent optimizer analysis work have shown that Adam's per-parameter learning rate effectively varies across the accumulation window, meaning a domain-heavy tail in accumulation produces parameter-wise rate inflation for domain-relevant weights at exactly the moment the general-data gradient would otherwise have dampened it. The clean fix is interleaving — alternating domain and general micro-batches within every accumulation window rather than concatenating them — but this requires explicit data pipeline engineering that most frameworks don't provide by default, and at large batch sizes (e.g., 4M tokens per step as in LLaMA-scale training) the logistics of guaranteed interleaving across distributed data loaders introduce non-trivial synchronization overhead. A subtler problem is that gradient accumulation simulates large batches but doesn't replicate them exactly under Adam, and the discrepancy grows with accumulation depth; at accumulation depths of 8–16 (common when training 70B models on memory-constrained hardware), the sequential bias can shift effective per-parameter learning rates by factors of 2–4x relative to a true large-batch step, which is larger than the LLRD decay factors practitioners typically tune. The deepest issue is that this makes the warmup geometry problem hardware-contingent: two teams training the same model with the same nominal hyperparameters but different accumulation depths and micro-batch orderings will produce meaningfully different weight trajectories during the critical first few hundred steps, making results difficult to reproduce or compare even when mixing ratios and learning rate schedules appear identical.

The danger of a cold start (resetting v_t to zero) is that Adam's effective learning rate for each parameter is 1/sqrt(v_t + ε), so at initialization v_t ≈ 0 and every parameter gets a near-maximum effective rate simultaneously — this is why learning rate warmup was invented in the first place, but when combined with a cold optimizer the warmup schedule and the v_t buildup are racing each other, and in the first few hundred steps before v_t stabilizes the effective per-parameter rates can spike 10–50x above their eventual steady-state values for weights with small gradients. Partial decay — multiplying v_t by a factor between 0.5 and 0.9 before domain adaptation begins — is a middle path that deliberately inflates effective learning rates modestly for high-curvature general-pretraining weights while avoiding the full cold-start pathology; this is analogous to learning rate rewinding in lottery ticket literature but operating on optimizer state rather than weights. The interaction with warmup geometry is sharp: a short aggressive warmup with a warm optimizer is relatively safe because v_t dampens the worst parameter-wise excursions, but a short aggressive warmup with a cold or partially decayed optimizer is maximally dangerous — the two sources of rate inflation compound multiplicatively rather than canceling, and the result is a brief window of effective learning rates that no nominal schedule would ever intentionally prescribe.

The low-rank gradient subspace idea has direct published support: Gradient Episodic Memory and its descendant GradProject work by projecting updates orthogonal to a remembered gradient basis, and the key insight from Saha et al. (2021) in "Gradient Projection Memory for Continual Learning" is that you only need to retain the top-k singular vectors of the gradient matrix from previous tasks — empirically k=50–200 captures enough of the interference-causing subspace for vision and NLP tasks at moderate scale, and the projection cost is O(k·d) per layer rather than O(d²), which is the difference between feasible and prohibitive. Extending this to LLM scale requires computing those singular vectors from a sample of general-pretraining gradients, which means one SVD per weight matrix per layer — expensive but a one-time offline cost, and recent work on gradient compression for distributed training suggests the top-20 singular vectors capture 60–80% of gradient variance in transformer MLP blocks, meaning a rank-20 projection barrier might provide most of the protection at modest memory overhead. LoRA's subspace structure does accidentally provide a partial version of this, but with an important inversion: LoRA constrains domain adaptation updates to live within a low-rank subspace (the BA product), whereas what you want for interference prevention is updates constrained to live outside the general-pretraining gradient subspace — these are geometrically opposite constraints, so naively applied LoRA doesn't give you projection protection and may actually concentrate domain updates in exactly the subspace directions most likely to interfere. However, there's a non-obvious way LoRA helps indirectly: if you initialize LoRA adapters such that their span is orthogonal to the top singular vectors of the general-pretraining gradient (which you can enforce at initialization by projecting the random B matrix), you get approximate gradient orthogonality for free throughout training without any per-step projection cost — this is the idea behind orthogonal LoRA variants like OFT (Orthogonal Fine-Tuning, Qiu et al., 2023) and GS-LoRA, though neither was designed explicitly for continual pretraining interference. The residual gap is that LoRA's rank is fixed at initialization while the dangerous gradient subspace evolves during the warmup window as domain gradients reshape the weight matrices — a static orthogonal initialization provides a one-time barrier but doesn't track the drifting interference subspace, meaning protection degrades across the warmup window precisely when the domain corpus is accumulating its strongest directional pressure on the weights.
